content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes PT2, a human pose transfer method that permutes the textures at random and reconstructs the image with dual branch attention. The experiment results demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The permutation process is interesting.
2. The experiment results look nice and generally demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
3. The writing is clear and easy to follow.

Weakness:
1. Concerns of the Pose Branch design.
    - As mentioned in the Texture Branch motivation, the random permutation breaks the structure information. Will this damage the structure information in the Pose Branch?
    - I see the "w/o. Pose Branch" in the ablation study. It would be better for me to see the performance of a "w/ structure maintained Pose Branch".
2. Details on the Permutation.
    - Do you put the patches in a large canvas?
    - Why not concat them channel-wise, which would easily alleviate the field overlap problem?
3. Details on the Dual Branch Attention module.
    - How do you combine the outputs of the two transformers to obtain the new T?
    - What is the detail operation of the residual block?
4. Lack of analysis on the patch size k. 
    - How do you determine the proper patch size k?
    - How does k affect the final performance when it varies from 1 to the image size?
    - It would be great to see more analysis of it.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3352 by Reviewer eH62

content.title: Author Responses
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments, we address your concerns as follows:
>1:  Concerns of the Pose Branch design.

> -As mentioned in the Texture Branch motivation, the random permutation breaks the structure information. Will this damage the structure information in the Pose Branch?

Response:   Yes, it will also permute the structure in the pose branch. 
>-I see the "w/o. Pose Branch" in the ablation study. It would be better for me to see the performance of a "w/ structure maintained Pose Branch".

Response:   "w/o. Input Permuting" in Table 4 removes the input permuting for both branches, which preserves the structure of pose and thus is the same as "w/ structure maintained Pose Branch”. Note that it’s not possible to keep the pose structure and only permute the texture because the pose and texture feature maps have to be spatially aligned in the attention module.

>2:   Details on the Permutation.

>Do you put the patches in a large canvas?

Response: Mostly yes, but the size of the canvas depends on the size of the original image and of the patch. If the image size is divisible by the patch size, then the canvas size is the same as the image size. Otherwise, for an image of size H x W and a patch of size p x p, the canvas is of size p$\cdot$ceil(H/p) $\times$ p$\cdot$ceil(W/p), where ceil() is the least integer function.

>Why not concatenate them channel-wise, which would easily alleviate the field overlap problem?

Response: We do not concatenate the patches because channel-wise concatenation would limit the effective receptive field to be at most the patch size, meaning we can’t use a larger receptive field to learn more styles and patterns. We added an ablation of concatenating the patches in Table 4. As can be seen in Table 4, concatenating the patches degrades FID, SSIM and LPIPS compared to using dual-kernel encoder in our model.

>3: Details on the Dual Branch Attention module.

>-How do you combine the outputs of the two transformers to obtain the new T?

Response: The outputs are concatenated to obtain new T.
>-What is the in-detail operation of the residual block?

Response: The residual block is the same as the commonly-used one in the resnet paper, which includes a skip connection and two convolutional layers.  It’s formulated as 

$\text{Res}(T_i)=f_i(z)\cdot {h_i}(T_{i})+g_i(z)+{h_i^{skip}}(T_{i})$

where $f_i,g_i,h_i,h_i^{skip}$ are learnable functions.

>4: Lack of analysis on the patch size k.

Response: Thank you for the suggestion.  We found a smaller patch size strengthens the disentanglement but also causes more field overlapping. A larger patch size has less field overlapping but leads to more entangled pose and texture. To balance the two factors, we conducted more ablation experiments on the patch size and found our model gets best performance with a batch size of 16, the largest decrease in performance coming from using a patch size of 256 (i.e., image size).

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a pose transfer network that takes the permuted textures of the original person image as inputs and generates the person at the target pose.

The highlight of the proposed framework is that different kernel sizes and attentions are employed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:

1) The paper is easy to follow and well-written.
2) It is reasonable to perturb the source images at the image level rather than at the feature level in order to better disentangle the pose information and texture information.
3) Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method quantitatively and qualitatively.

Weaknesses:
1) The proposed techniques are somewhat trivial. It is just a mix of multiple attention mechanisms, and the attention mechanisms are already quite popular in the current pose transfer papers.
2) Ablation study is required to verify if the human parsing part is necessary to be fed into the network as an input.

>1: The proposed techniques are just a mix of multiple attention mechanisms, and the attention mechanisms are already quite popular in the current pose transfer papers.

Response: Thank you for giving us an opportunity to clarify our contributions.  As explained in the introduction, our primary contribution is to achieve image-level disentanglement by permuting textures. Different kernel sizes and the attention mechanism are introduced to solve the problems caused by such permutation. Specifically, we found using dual kernels can reduce the noise caused by adjacent permuted patches, and the pose branch in the attention mechanism can recover clothing shape from the permuted textures.

>2: Ablation study is required to verify if the human parsing part is necessary to be fed into the network as an input.

Response: Thank you for these suggestions.  We found that when adding an ablation of removing human parsing maps to Table 4, our full model still improves all the metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed input permuting function.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The task this paper attempts to solve is human pose transfer, and specifically, in the scenario when no paired-data (of the same human in different poses) is available during training (which is a setting I find artificial). The key idea is to permute textures of the source image during training so as to train the model to self-reconstruct. Automatic quantitative evaluation and user studies comparing with prior work are included, although I am not currently convinced by the results due to lack of clarity of the experiment setting and metrics.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strength]

Figures in the paper are well-scaled and drawn with readable font sizes and image resolutions. Extensive comparison with previous work is conducted on 2 public datasets. 

[Weakness]

I am not entirely certain about the motivation of the approach, specifically, why paired-data of the same person in different poses is labor intensive to collect. DeepFashion is a dataset collected from online shopping sites while Market-1501 from surveillance video; either source is easily accessible and comes in large-scale. It makes more sense to me for the approach to jointly train paired-data with unpaired-data than completely ignoring largely accessible paired-data. Training without paired-data seems to me an artificial task to begin with.

I find the evaluation not particularly convincing. First is the numbers for SSIM, FID, LPIPS, IS (Table 1, 2): they are mainly for measuring "overall" quality of the synthesized images, but there is no answer to questions like: exactly how much improvement actually translates to human's perception, or which specific aspect the improvement comes from, etc. Without knowing the answers to the above questions, it is hard for readers to interpret that the improved numbers are meaningful on the task of human pose transfer. Even if improved numbers have been previously accepted as better human perception, is it guaranteed that this relation continues to hold true "linearly" as the numbers improve? Moreover, I wasn't able to find anywhere in the paper the definition of what a hundred percent success of human pose transfer looks like. Currently I suppose it should consider a combination of the following factors: human's facial identity (whether or not to include hairstyle), authenticity of the clothes the human wears (which is more important, the shape of the clothes or the texture of the clothes), perfect realism of individual parts (from face to hair to clothes to body parts); but exactly, what are the importance weights of the above listed items? In the qualitative figures in the paper, for some examples I see the clothes texture being perfect while shape has changed, for some I see artifacts on hands or legs while clothes look fine, for some the hairstyle has completely changed, etc., which of these cases are more successful than the others? It would be more helpful of the community to focus on where to improve for the task of human pose transfer if the evaluation metrics were able to give a clearer direction on which factors are most important in this task and which need most improvement in a quantifiable way. I have similar questions for the user study (Table 3) as well: from the paper's writing, it reads like the question for subjects was "which image looks most similar to the true image". Again, it is unclear whether image A with more authentic texture or image B with more authentic shape is more similar to ground-truth. It would've been more informative if the interests of similarity in the context of this task were first defined and then listed out as individual questions to the human subject, like: "which image preserves the human's facial identity better?", "which image has clothes more similar to the true image with respect to texture", "which image generates overall least artifacts?", etc.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The authors include the original source code for the proposed method, making it reproducible (although I have not actually tested the code). The approach section is written in a fairly clear way. Since there are some key questions unanswered for me regarding the experiment results (as discussed in the Strength and Weakness section), I currently don't find the quality particularly high.
content.summary_of_the_review: While extensive comparison with previous work is conducted on 2 public datasets, I find it hard to interpret the claimed better numbers given that the success of human pose transfer was never defined in the paper and how these numbers scale to readers' perception of the qualitative results is unclear. Based on the the paper's current status, I recommend a rejection for now.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3352 by Reviewer GVhe

content.title: Author Responses
content.comment:
>1: why paired-data of the same person in different poses is labor intensive to collect. DeepFashion is a dataset collected from online shopping sites while Market-1501 from surveillance video; either source is easily accessible and comes in large-scale.

Response: First of all, fashion trends change fast in a short period of time. When collecting new datasets of fashion models, it is cheaper to collect unpaired images than paired ones.In addition, collecting paired data of the same person requires that the paired images are under the same background and lighting conditions. Otherwise, in a dataset like Market-1501, where the paired image has different background and lighting, training with these images is much more difficult as shown in Table 2. On the other hand, unpaired images do not have these restrictions and thus are much easier to collect.

>2: It would've been more informative if the interests of similarity in the context of this task were first defined and then listed out as individual questions to the human subject.

Response: Projecting each objective evaluation metric to human perception is an important and still on-developing topic in the research community. Since it is difficult to decide which aspect in the image can reflect the most important improvement on the task, we first followed prior work and chose overall evaluation metrics (e.g., SSIM, LPIPS and etc. ) for a fair comparison, and then we conducted human evaluations. The actual question we asked the user is “Compare the person's clothing textures, choose the image that looks more similar to the ground truth picture.”  However, as you suggested, this just reflects the texture correctness of the generated image. Therefore, we redesigned the experiments and asked the user to evaluate the quality of the generated images in the following three aspects: texture correctness, facial identity preservation and plausibility. The updated results are provided in Table 3 of the revised manuscript. Our model consistently outperforms prior methods that are trained without paired data on all three aspects.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the pose transfer problem by proposing a novel self-driven method. Authors argue that existing methods disentangle pose and texture in feature-level, resulting in loss of details and unwanted artifacts. To solve the problem, they provide a dual-branch framework to achieve image-level disentanglement without using paired images for supervision. In each branch, the input permutation and different kernel sizes are introduced to improve the performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The paper is generally well written. The problem to address and the shortcomings of the existing approaches are discussed well. 
2. This paper designs a self-driven method that only requires the source pose in the training process, which gets rid of the requirement of paired data. Besides, it provides a new idea to permutate input for disentangling the texture and pose in the image-level.
Weaknesses:
1. The novelty should be claimed clearly. Specifically, although the authors named the two branches "pose branch" and "texture branch", the network components in both branches seem to be the same except for the inputs. Perhaps the authors should elaborate on the particular design for pose and texture.
2. The multi-kernel design is a common motivation and not novel enough. The techniques employed are not that advanced.
3. The details of qualitative results are confusing. For example, in Figures 5 and 7, although PT² achieves good performance in clothes, the other details (e.g., hair and shoes) differ from the source and target images.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is overall well written with sufficient details. It feels like not too hard to reproduce while reading the paper. The main idea is clearly explained with proper illustrations.
content.summary_of_the_review: As mentioned above, the paper checks all the boxes necessary for a computer vision paper and seems to be working well. However, it has some issues in terms of novelty and evaluation.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3352 by Reviewer ZbXV

content.title: Author Responses
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments, we address your concerns as follows:

>1: The novelty should be claimed clearly. Specifically, although the authors named the two branches "pose branch" and "texture branch", the network components in both branches seem to be the same except for the inputs. Perhaps the authors should elaborate on the particular design for pose and texture.

Response: Thank you for giving us the opportunity to clarify our contributions.  First, we would like to note that our primary contribution is learning to disentangle pose from texture by permuting the images and then learning to reconstruct them.  For the dual branch design, we created a new pose branch to give a texture-agnostic initialization of the learned pose transformation and gradually integrate the textures in the learned transformation function. Compared to prior work which combines the pose and texture in one branch to transfer textures, we find our pose branch better recovers shape and length information. The architectural designs for both branches are the same in order to make the texture and pose feature maps have exactly the same receptive field and thus be spatially aligned in the attention module. These explanations have been added accordingly to the revised manuscript.

>2: The multi-kernel design is a common motivation and not novel enough. The techniques employed are not that advanced.

Response: We agree that  our contribution for the multi-kernel design could have been explained more clearly. Our contribution is not proposing the multi-kernel module, but showing that this module is effective in reducing the noise caused by permutations of patches. We have revised our descriptions in the manuscript accordingly.

>3: The details of qualitative results are confusing. For example, in Figures 5 and 7, although PT² achieves good performance in clothes, the other details (e.g., hair and shoes) differ from the source and target images.

Response: Thank you for giving us the opportunity to improve our approach’s description and clarify our analysis. In a pose transfer task, what the person would like in a different pose has multiple reasonable solutions, and the given ground truth is only one of them. For example, if the image of the source person’s front view does not show shoes, the shoes are unknown objects and thus could be of any color and type in the person’s full body view. Floating and occluded objects such as hair have the same issue since we can only infer the appearance of these objects in a completely different view.Therefore, in Figure 5 and 7, the target image in the dataset should  just be a reference of what the image would look like after pose transfer. Since this could be misleading, we changed the target image to the target pose in the revised manuscript.
